h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר י״ב Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Yud Bais

p: In the Yotzer for the blessing of Krias Shema
everyone who passed through her sea —
let them weigh out a shekel without confusion,
עַל שֵׁם הַכָּתוּב [שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ה, ב]
גַּם מַה שֶּׁאָמַר כָּל הָעוֹבֵר בְּיַמָּה
but also what he says, "everyone who passed through her sea" —
what connection there is to mention here
And indeed in the Zohar Chadash
(beginning of Parshas Ki Sisa) too it states:
they drew close to one another;
then they are called "the holy shekel,"
because He is half a body
and Knesses Yisrael is half a body;
they joined one with the other,
יַנְקִין כָּל חַד מֵאֲתַר דִּילֵיהּ וְכוּלֵּי
nurse, each one from its own place, etc. —
here too there is mention of the tribes
But the matter is as we said,
as one who transgressed the commandments of his Master, etc.,
that the shekalim came to atone for the sin of the Calf
and also to atone for the sale of Yosef,
which is the blemish in the aspect of Tzaddik —
in line with the two opinions
[שְׁקָלִים פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ג ט, ב]
that the shekalim came to atone for both,
since both corruptions are kept for the generations.
for from the blemish of the serpent
sprouted the blemish of the bris,
through the filth he cast into Chavah.
was undone what had been rectified
of the serpent's blemish at Matan Torah:
And the shekalim came to bring "zeh" close to "zos,"
to rectify the blemish of the bris,
and so the blemish of the Calf is also rectified,
for it is all one, as stated
And this is why he says "to the dove who is perfect,"
עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נג, ב)
that Knesses Yisrael is likened to a dove, etc.,
for she does not abandon her mate,
(וְכֵן הוּא בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ד, ב)
(and so it is in Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:2);
and as they said in the Zohar Chadash:
they joined one with the other,
And he says "everyone who passed through her sea,"
for in truth at Yetzias Mitzrayim,
at the Plague of the Firstborn,
as has been explained many times
that the plagues corresponded to the ten sefiros
in the aspect of "smiting for Mitzrayim
for afterward, at the Splitting of the Sea,
"and the water was a wall for them," spelled defectively,
do not read "chomah," wall, but "cheimah," wrath,
for there was anger against Yisrael,
as the angel of Mitzrayim accused:
"these are worshippers of stars and constellations," etc.
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב קע, ב).
But at the Splitting of the Sea,
as it states (in the Mechilta, Beshalach, HaShirah 3,
וְזֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק ב סד, ב)
a maidservant saw at the Sea
דְּאַף שֶׁנִּסְתַּר מֵהֶם הָאוֹר אַחַר כָּךְ
for although the light was hidden from them afterward,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶה נִשְׁאַר לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד
the longing to see the light;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב ס, א)
as they said in the holy Zohar (II 60a):
to gaze upon the radiance of the King's glory, etc.;
they said, what is the reason?
their souls were not sweetened as before, etc.;
the accuser was turned into a defender;
"There He set for it a statute" —
as they said in the Mechilta (Beshalach, Vayisa 1);
that is, there is a mitzvah
in which are Midrash, halachos and aggados,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה מו, א; מז, ז)
And this is what he says:
let them weigh out a shekel without confusion,
the root of the serpent's blemish is rectified,
which caused the blemish of the bris,
and through this they came to Mitzrayim
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ד, כה)
and all the males were fenced in from immorality in his merit.
And likewise the blemish of the Calf is rectified,
the corruption and blemish of the serpent.
וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן הַמְכֻוָּן בַּזֹּהַר חָדָשׁ
And this too is the intent in the Zohar Chadash,
in what they said, "the body was completed,
for from then on the longing remained, as mentioned above.
And Shabbos, being in the secret of the bris
is the time to rectify the blemish of the bris,
as has been explained many times;
through the reading of the parshah of Shekalim,
דְּאִיתָא בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה [פֶּרֶק ה מִשְׁנָה ג]
for it states in Sefer Yetzirah (chapter 5, mishnah 3)
that it was formed with the letter tzaddi,
in which is the time to rectify
the blemish in the aspect of Tzaddik.
וְאַף בְּחָל רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר בְּשַׁבָּת
And even when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbos,
that the holiness of Shabbos is
in accordance with the preparation of the weekdays
and the weekdays before Parshas Shekalim
which is designated for the rectification of the attribute of Tzaddik,
which was formed with the letter kuf (Sefer Yetzirah ibid.),
and it is designated for the eradication of Amalek,
who is the opposite of the holiness of the attribute of Tzaddik,
as has been explained many times.
And it is the preparation for the month of Nissan,
שֶׁבּוֹ עֲתִידִין לְהִגָּאֵל [רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יא, א]:
in which they are destined to be redeemed (Rosh Hashanah 11a).

paragraphs.text: Yotzer for Parshas Shekalim, El Mitnasse Lechol Lerosh, stanzas beginning Yachid Shokhen Romah and Kol HaOver BeYamah — “The Unique One who dwells on high stipulated in a perfect Torah for the dove that is pure: all who crossed the sea shall weigh out a shekel without commotion—a half-shekel as an offering.” Both the dove and the crossing of the sea occur in the original poem. Rav Tzadok develops the first through fidelity to the covenant and the second through the abiding desire awakened by the revelation at the sea.

paragraphs.text: Song of Songs 5:2 — “I was asleep, but my heart was awake. The voice of my beloved knocks: Open for me, my sister, my companion, my dove, my perfect one; for my head is filled with dew, my locks with the drops of the night.” The verse joins the two names that Rav Tzadok hears in the liturgical description: the dove and the perfect or whole one.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 53b:19 — “Why specifically a dove? Because the Congregation of Israel is compared to a dove, as it is written, ‘The wings of the dove are covered with silver, and her pinions with greenish gold.’ Just as a dove is saved only by its wings, so Israel are saved only through the commandments.” This supplies the identification of the dove with Israel. Its marital faithfulness is established by the following rabbinic sources.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 100b:29; Rashi, s.v. “ve-arayot mi-yonah” — “Rabbi Yohanan said: Had the Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, avoidance of theft from the ant, and avoidance of forbidden sexual relations from the dove.” Rashi explains “forbidden sexual relations from the dove”: “It mates only with its own partner.” The comparison concerns fidelity to the particular bond, which is central to Rav Tzadok’s account of covenantal repair.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:1, “Your eyes are doves” — “Just as this dove is modest, so Israel are modest. ... Just as this dove, once it recognizes its mate, never exchanges it for another, so Israel, once they recognized the Holy One, blessed be He, did not exchange Him for another.” The division cited as 4:2 in the manuscript appears within the exposition of “Your eyes are doves” in the present digital division, 4:1. The same passage appears in 1:15.

paragraphs.text: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Vayehi Beshalach 7:7 — “‘The children of Israel walked on dry land within the sea.’ The ministering angels were astonished. They said: Master of all worlds! Human beings who worship idols are walking on dry land within the sea! From where do we know that the sea too became filled with anger against them? Above it says ‘hemah,’ and so it says ‘homah.’ What caused them to be saved? ‘On their right and on their left’: on their right, through the merit of Torah, as it is said, ‘From His right hand a fiery law for them’; and on their left, prayer.” The source contrasts the defective spelling of the word for a wall with the word for anger. In the retrieved tractate division this appears in Vayehi Beshalach 7, rather than chapter 6.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 170b, Terumah 84:4–5 — “When Israel approached the sea and the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to divide the Sea of Reeds for them, Rahab, the prince appointed over Egypt, came and demanded judgment before the Holy One. He said: Master of the world! Why do You wish to execute judgment upon Egypt and divide the sea for Israel? All of them are guilty before You, and all Your ways are justice and truth. These worship the stars and constellations, and those worship the stars and constellations; these commit sexual transgressions, and those commit sexual transgressions; these shed blood, and those shed blood. At that moment it was difficult before Him to pass beyond the way of judgment. ... Had the Holy One not regarded the merit of Abraham, who rose early to perform his Master’s command and will, all of them would have been lost in the sea.” This is the precise accusation invoked here; the obstacle is the claim of strict judgment, rather than an inability to divide water.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 40 — “Although afterward it was hidden from them… at least the longing and desire remained… at first Hashem shows a person, as a loan, what he can later attain through his toil, and then removes that light so that he acquire it by his labor.” Rav Tzadok there explains why the desire left by Kerias Yam Suf is what leads to the acquisition at Sinai.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 60a, Beshalach 25:11–13 — “When they finished the words, all of them were filled with delight in their souls and longed to see and contemplate. They did not wish to move from there because of the greatness of their longing. At that hour Moses said to the Holy One, blessed be He: Your children, in their great longing to gaze upon You, do not wish to move away from the sea. ... They did not set out until Moses took hold of them and showed them the radiance of the glory of the Holy One in the wilderness. Then, because of their great longing and desire to contemplate, Moses led them onward. ... What is the wilderness of Shur? The wilderness in which they wished to contemplate the glorious radiance of the Holy King. Therefore it is called the wilderness of Shur: contemplation was there.” The source explains their departure through continuing desire for the revelation, the enduring element Rav Tzadok distinguishes from the passing experience.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 60a–b, Beshalach 26:3–4 — “While they were walking in the wilderness, another domain, that of the other nations, was revealed against them—the power that rules in the wilderness—and they encountered it there. Israel saw that their King’s glorious radiance was no longer there. ... Why ‘for they were bitter’? Their souls were no longer delighted as before; furthermore, it came to accuse them. ... ‘The Lord showed him a tree’: a tree means Torah, as it is written, ‘She is a tree of life to those who hold fast to her.’ ... When the radiance of their King’s glory was revealed to them, then ‘he cast it into the water, and the water became sweet.’ What is meant by ‘the water became sweet’? The accuser became an advocate.” The bitterness and its sweetening continue the account of the hidden and restored radiance.

paragraphs.text: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Vayassa 1:19 — “‘There He established for him a statute and a judgment’: ‘a statute’—this is Shabbat; ‘a judgment’—this is honoring father and mother. These are the words of Rabbi Joshua. Rabbi Elazar of Modiin says: ‘a statute’ means the forbidden sexual relationships ... and ‘a judgment’ means the laws concerning coercion, penalties, and injuries.” Rav Tzadok follows Rabbi Joshua’s interpretation of the statute at Marah as Shabbat.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 46:1; 47:7 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Do not be distressed over the first tablets, for they contained only the Ten Commandments. With the second tablets I am giving you laws, midrash, and aggadot. This is what is written, ‘He would tell you the hidden things of wisdom, for wisdom is doubled.’ Moreover, you are thereby informed that I have forgiven your sin, as it is said, ‘Know that God has set aside part of your iniquity.’” Shemot Rabbah 47:7 repeats the contrast and specifies that laws, midrash, aggadot, and Talmud are to remain oral. The expansion after the sin is therefore part of the cited Midrash itself.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:12:1 — “Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: Sarah went down to Egypt and fenced herself off from sexual transgression, and all the women were protected through her merit. Joseph went down to Egypt and fenced himself off from sexual transgression, and all the males were protected through his merit. Rabbi Phinehas said in the name of Rabbi Hiyya: This protection against sexual transgression was by itself sufficient merit for Israel to be redeemed from Egypt.” The manuscript’s older section reference 4:25 corresponds to the exposition of “A locked garden,” here divided as 4:12:1.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sod Yesharim, Parshas Shekalim 1 — “The half-shekel shows that Yisrael recognize they have no completeness of their own without Hashem; and Hashem likewise says there is no completeness to the honor of Heaven without the service of Yisrael; their union is called a whole shekel.” The Radziner gives the inner meaning of the Zohar Chadash’s “half a body”: each half becomes whole only through the other.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 44a, Tazria 9:6 — “This offering is like the animal offering: this is after eight days, and that is after eight days, as it is written, ‘From the eighth day onward it will be accepted.’ Through what is it accepted? By one Shabbat having passed over it. Once one Shabbat has passed over it, this one is acceptable as an offering, and that one is acceptable as an offering. Why? Because it has become attached and joined to that Shabbat, the mystery of the holy covenant. Therefore everything is in a supernal mystery.” The source links both circumcision on the eighth day and the animal’s eligibility for sacrifice with encountering Shabbat.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Shevat 2 — “The letter tzadi indicates the midda of tzaddik… ‘a bent tzaddik, an upright tzaddik’: at first he must be bent, fighting with strength to bend the yetzer to good; afterward upright, meriting to straighten the heart.” This shows the work of Shevat that prepares Parshas Shekalim: the repair of yesod proceeds from conquering the yetzer to a heart made wholly straight.

paragraphs.text: Sefer Yetzirah 5, month-letter correspondences — “He made the letter tzadi rule, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Aquarius in the world, Shevat in the year, and the stomach in the person. He made the letter kuf rule, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Pisces in the world, Adar in the year, and the gizzard in the person.” The month-letter correspondences are explicit in the retrieved Warsaw 1884 text, divided as 5:2. Their use as preparation for repairing the quality of the righteous one is Rav Tzadok’s exposition.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 104a:7 — “Kuf—holy; resh—wicked. Why does the kuf turn its face away from the resh? The Holy One, blessed be He, says: I cannot look upon a wicked person. Why is the crown of the kuf turned toward the resh? The Holy One says: If he returns, I will bind a crown upon him like Mine. Why does the leg of the kuf hang apart? So that if he returns, he may enter.” The alphabetic exposition gives kuf its association with holiness while preserving an entrance for repentance.

The Holy One says: If he returns, I will bind a crown upon him like Mine. Why does the leg of the kuf hang apart? So that if he returns, he may enter.” The alphabetic exposition gives kuf its association with holiness while preserving an entrance for repentance.
